clue.text: 5th to 15th century: quietly study expanding corporation

parts.note: the Middle Ages is the period of European history roughly from the 5th to the 15th century
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, quietly
to read is to study, as in reading law

explanation.surface: A history note on the medieval period followed by advice to study quietly about a growing company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is an old jokey word for a paunch, so an expanding corporation is a growing belly, not a growing business.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporation is a dated humorous word for a pot belly, and the spread of the waistline in midlife is exactly that belly growing.

clue.text: Does a second job performing at a popular classical piece

parts.note: to moonlight is to work a second job on the side, often unofficially
a performer on stage is said to be on
taken as written

explanation.surface: A musician who takes extra gigs plays a well-known classical favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 is nicknamed this and is among the best-known works in the classical repertoire.

clue.text: Being what England expected of the French one in rising German air

parts.note: du is French for 'of the'

indicators.note: the letter for one is placed inside the reversed German word
in a down clue, rising means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: Luft is the German word for air
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A patriotic line about Nelson's England mixed with French and German phrases about the air.
explanation.walkthrough: Nelson's signal at Trafalgar was 'England expects that every man will do his duty'. In a down clue 'rising' turns LUFT into TFUL, and I goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson's signal said England expected every man to do his duty, so meeting that expectation is being dutiful, obedient to duty.

clue.text: Just so restrained in modern style gathering

parts.note: lite is the modern marketing spelling of light, meaning toned down or restrained
a rally is a mass gathering of people

explanation.surface: A remark about a fashionable gathering that stays tasteful and understated.
explanation.walkthrough: LITE is 'light' spelt in the modern commercial style, as in lite beer; light here is restrained, low-key.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally means exactly as stated, word for word, which is the sense of 'just so' as precisely that way.

clue.text: Big hole in baby's sock

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the run of letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A child's sock has worn through with a huge hole.
explanation.definitionFit: An abyss is a deep chasm or bottomless pit, a very large hole in the ground.

clue.text: Prize-winning Egyptian island with right and wrong idea

parts.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island where Napoleon was exiled

indicators.note: the letters of the following word are put the wrong way, rearranged

explanation.surface: An Egyptian laureate is described via an island holiday and a muddled notion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prize-winning' points to the Nobel Peace Prize, which the Egyptian diplomat shared in 2005; 'wrong' gives the rearranged letters ADEI.
explanation.definitionFit: Mohamed ElBaradei, the Egyptian head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, shared the 2005 Nobel Peace Prize.

clue.text: Easter party leader as companion

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: taken as written
CH is the abbreviation for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A festive gathering for Easter is led by a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British honour, so 'companion' gives those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasch is an old word for the Passover and for Easter, from the Hebrew pesach via Latin pascha.

clue.text: Retire discomfited to a country in Africa

indicators.note: discomfited means thrown into disorder, so the letters of the preceding word are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An embarrassed person retreats to an African nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discomfited' gives the rearranged letters ERITRE, and 'to' only joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eritrea is a nation on the Red Sea coast of the Horn of Africa, independent from Ethiopia since 1993.

clue.text: Accident blackspot where rage and contempt are both within our editor's wayward grasp

indicators.note: both of the words for rage and contempt are put inside the jumbled letters
a grasp holds something inside it, so the scrambled letters close round the word for rage
wayward means going astray, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: ED is the usual abbreviation for editor
anger is rage
scorn is contempt

explanation.surface: An editor angrily dismisses a notorious stretch of road where crashes happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wayward' gives DOUER; 'grasp' and 'are both within' set the two words inside it. Dangerous Corner is also a J. B. Priestley play, fitting the setter's film-and-stage name.
explanation.definitionFit: A dangerous corner is a bend in a road where crashes often happen, the very picture of an accident blackspot.

clue.text: Something to do with one's welcome exposes river

definitions.text: Something to do with one's welcome

parts.note: to out someone is to expose them publicly
the Tay is the longest river in Scotland

explanation.surface: A remark on hospitality that drifts into revealing a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to the idiom 'outstay one's welcome', meaning to remain as a guest too long.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is to outstay one's welcome, remaining longer than a host wants, so the verb is what one does with a welcome.

clue.text: Strong point — it's good to drink wine

indicators.note: to drink is to take in, so the wine goes inside

parts.note: c'est bon, 'it's good' in French, gives bon
Asti is an Italian sparkling wine

explanation.surface: Someone praises the restorative power of a glass of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's good' leans on French, c'est bon, rather than an English synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A bastion is a projecting part of a fortification, and figuratively any stronghold or strong point of a belief.

clue.text: One with long sentence reactionary judge has mistakenly reduced

indicators.note: reactionary suggests going back, so the whole run is read backwards

parts.note: a ref, short for referee, judges a game

indicators.note: reduced means cut short by its last letter

parts.note: ill as an adverb means badly or mistakenly, as in ill-advised

explanation.surface: A hardline judge wrongly cuts a criminal's sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' makes IL, and 'reactionary' turns REFIL round; the surface's judge cutting a sentence is a decoy for the prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner serving a life term is called a lifer, and a life term is the longest of sentences.

clue.text: More to pay for tea during rapid increase

indicators.note: during places the tea in the middle of the increase

parts.note: a surge is a sudden sharp rise
char is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: A price note about tea costs shooting up.
explanation.walkthrough: CHAR is everyday British slang for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A surcharge is an extra fee added on top of the usual price, so it is an additional amount owed.

clue.text: Dramatic accompaniment to arsenic between strings made of precious metal thread

indicators.note: the play's words sit between two letters standing for strings

parts.note: G and D are strings of a violin
Arsenic and Old Lace is a famous stage comedy, so old lace goes with arsenic in the theatre

explanation.surface: A theatre prop of poisonous intent is set between violin strings and finished with gilt.
explanation.walkthrough: G and D are two of the four violin strings, and they enclose OLD LACE from the play Arsenic and Old Lace.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold-laced describes cloth trimmed with lace woven from gold thread, as on military dress uniforms.

clue.text: Channel island ape a little changed by a little smoke

parts.note: CI is the abbreviation for Channel Islands

indicators.note: the word for the ape is altered slightly, its letters rearranged

parts.note: a gorilla is a great ape

explanation.surface: An ape from the Channel Islands takes up smoking a small cigar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a little changed' rearranges GORILLA as GARILLO by swapping its O and A.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarillo is a small thin cigar, so smoking one is having a little smoke.

clue.text: State in which I had a house

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a US state where they once owned a home.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is a US state in the Pacific Northwest, famous for its potatoes.

clue.text: Awfully fine story that can't be put into words

definitions.text: that can't be put into words

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: a fable is a short moral story

explanation.surface: A tale so wonderfully good that it defies description.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully' rearranges FINE as INEF.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineffable means too great or extreme to be expressed in language, beyond description.

clue.text: Unknown likeness backed by 1 over 8

indicators.note: backed means turned back, so the word is written in reverse

parts.note: spit, as in the spit and image, is an exact likeness
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A mysterious resemblance supported by an obscure fraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for slightly drunk, having one drink beyond eight pints; 'backed' turns SPIT to TIPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Slightly drunk is the meaning of the British idiom one over the eight, so the cross-referenced numbers make a fitting synonym.

clue.text: Newspaper editor's trousers looking ok?

parts.note: the press is newspapers collectively
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A journalist's boss checks whether their trousers look smart.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: trousers look neat when ironed with a crease.
explanation.definitionFit: Trousers look smart when ironed with a sharp crease, which is having been pressed.

clue.text: Crazy American soldier subdued by new-fangled transport

indicators.note: crazy suggests something wild, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: GI is the usual term for an American soldier

explanation.surface: A deranged GI is overpowered aboard a modern vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' rearranges GI with SUBDUED as one pool of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A guided bus runs on a dedicated concrete track that steers it, a relatively recent form of public transport.

clue.text: Titled man with a single exception at the top

parts.note: bar one means except for one, with a single exception

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is taken, the one found at its head

explanation.surface: A nobleman unique in standing above everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: BAR ONE means 'except one'; the T is the first letter of 'top'.
explanation.definitionFit: A baronet holds a hereditary British title ranking below a baron, addressed as Sir.

clue.text: Green gets hour in court, returning for extra run

indicators.note: the colour and the hour go inside the word for court
returning means going back, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: to woo is to court a lover
vert is the heraldic word for green

explanation.surface: An inexperienced person gets an hour in court, then comes back for more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' makes OOW. In cricket an overthrow is a run scored when a fielder's throw goes past the stumps; 'Green' looks like a novice but is heraldic colour.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket an overthrow is an extra run taken when a fielder's return throw misses the stumps and runs away.

clue.text: Course for voice

definitions.meaning: the high adult male singing voice

explanation.definitionFit: Tenor means both the settled course of something and the male voice range above baritone.

clue.text: Water supplies greatly progress in American company

parts.note: wells supply water from underground
far means by a great deal, as in far better
to go is to progress or move on

explanation.surface: A firm's progress in the US depends greatly on its water sources.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells Fargo is a large US bank, founded as a stagecoach and express company in 1852.

clue.text: See 22
Supply of weapons and a lot of poison for a pound

indicators.note: a lot of, not all, so the end of the poison is cut off

parts.note: arsenic is a well-known poison
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone buys a large quantity of poison for a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of' leaves ARSEN, most but not all of the poison; 'for' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An arsenal is a store or collection of weapons and ammunition.

clue.text: Country of prohibition captured by Trotsky

indicators.note: captured by means held inside the name

parts.note: Leon Trotsky was the Russian revolutionary
a ban is a prohibition

explanation.surface: A Russian revolutionary seizes a nation known for its prohibition.
explanation.walkthrough: Trotsky's first name supplies the container, not his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Lebanon is a nation on the eastern Mediterranean coast, bordered by Syria and Israel.

clue.text: Aren't funny about Holderness characters getting protection in wartime

indicators.note: funny means odd, and about suggests turning round, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Residents of an English district protest about wartime defences.
explanation.walkthrough: Holderness is a coastal area of East Yorkshire; its letters with AREN'T are rearranged, 'characters' saying letters are used. An Anderson shelter was a corrugated-iron air-raid shelter dug into British gardens in World War II.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anderson shelter was a prefabricated garden air-raid shelter issued to British households to protect them from bombing during the Second World War.
